title.narrative: She Leads Kenya

description.narrative:
Currently we are witnessing a rise in girls and young women’s activism and protest. The She Leads programme will partner with existing GYW-led groups and feminist organizations. Importantly, special efforts are made to support existing informal groups of girls and young women, for example girls clubs, associations, student groups and unregistered organizations, which have started to organize and mobilize but are often excluded from many funding mechanisms.
In Kenya, the programme builds directly on the experiences of the previous Girls Advocacy Alliance (2016-2020).
FEMNET and DCI-ECPAT are network organisations, and will be working in all countries through selected members of their respective networks. Plan International and Terre des Hommes will work through their country offices and with local contracted organisations to implement projects under the overall She Leads programme. Finally, She Leads will seek alignment and collaboration with the Dutch Embassy and other consortiums funded under the Strengthening Civil Society framework of the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. In particular, She Leads will seek alignment with the four other consortiums funded under the Women’s Rights and Gender Equality (WRGE) theme of the Power of Voices funding mechanism.

Girls and young women’s (GYW’s) rights to engage in public decision-making are enshrined in international agreements and national laws. In reality, however, GYW voices are excluded from the socio-political domain, particularly those of GYW who experience intersecting forms of discrimination.
GYW’s meaningful participation is obstructed by three interrelated factors. Firstly, discriminatory gender- and age-related social norms limit GYW’s rights to move freely, voice opinions and engage in public life. Secondly, GYW groups in civil society are under resourced and lack strong ties with more established CSOs. The latter are not always responsive to the specific needs and perspectives of GYW-led groups. Furthermore, the global phenomenon of shrinking civic space is affecting GYW-led organizations, making it even harder for them to express their opinions, assemble and associate. Groups that challenge the ruling gender ideology are increasingly being intimidated, threatened and exposed to violence. In conflict and humanitarian contexts, GYW actors risk additional security threats as easy targets of militarized and extremist forces. Thirdly, political institutions at local and national level are dominated by elites consisting of mainly male, elder leaders, with no interest in institutional reforms that would make decision-making processes more inclusive, transparent and accountable. Existing consultation mechanisms (such as youth parliaments and advisory bodies) are usually poorly resourced, dependent on donor support and functioning irregularly.

SUMMARY In Kenya, girls and young women, particularly GYW from socially excluded and exploited groups, are denied the opportunity to voice their interests and to participate meaningfully in decision-making processes. While Kenya has made impressive strides in, for example, GYW’s access to education and the introduction of new laws against GBV, their socio-political participation continues to be much lower than that of boys and young men. Within the population of girls and young women (between age 14 till 24 years of age), there are specific groups of GYW in She Leads countries who suffer most from (intersectional) discrimination and exclusion. She Leads is a joint programme of Plan International Netherlands, Defence for Children - ECPAT the Netherlands (DCI-ECPAT), African Women’s Development and Communication Network (FEMNET), and Terre des Hommes the Netherlands (TdH). Equal Measures 2030 is a technical partner. In Kenya, She Leads members FEMNET, DCI-ECPAT, TdH and Plan will be implementing.

She Leads contributes to a lasting transformative effect on engagement of GYW in decision-making. The following strategies will be implemented:
1. Strengthening and resourcing GYW-led organizations: investing in the resource base of GYW-led organizations will help them access other funding in the future. 2. Support social movements: social movements can accelerate lasting change in societies’ structures and norms. She Leads will bring together child-rights and feminist organisations and GYW-led groups to push collectively for transformative change in gender norms, and for institutional reform. 3. Engaging boys & men, parents, and traditional and religious leaders: these actors are crucial allies to ensure structural change and permanent effects when it comes to norms change. Because of their status and their role in socialisation processes, these actors promote structural change in societies. 4. Engaging media: She Leads will use media as a tool to amplify GYWs voices, and will target media as a powerful agent of change. Opening space for GYW’s voices and leadership in the media will ultimately influence broader communities, and has lasting effects beyond the programme. 5. Organisational capacity strengthening of CSO’s: investments in advocacy capacity, building relationships with decision-makers, strengthening fundraising skills will have a lasting effect on their influencing work beyond She Leads. 6. Linking local, national, regional and global: She Leads is implemented at different levels that are strategically interconnected. Interventions and results in one domain trigger change in other domains, and changes at local, national, regional and international levels are connected and influence each other.

She Leads envisions change in 3 domains of society: the social-cultural, civil society and institutional domain. In the social-cultural domain, partners engage traditional and religious leaders, forging coalitions of progressive actors who, due to their status and authority, will galvanize their constituencies to adopt more positive gender and age norms. Awareness raising and diffusion of new ideas through media and peer networks (including boys and young men) will challenge existing norms and expectations. Young female activists play an important role in this process, by inspiring other girls and breaking down negative stereotypes. In the civil society domain, the creation (consolidation) of safe spaces in which GYW can meet, exchange, build their confidence, political consciousness and skills, is a major step towards increased self-organization. Another key condition is the increased capacity of (adult-led) CSOs to effectively support GYW collective action. Stronger collaboration between GYW groups, child and women’s rights networks will lead to a more enabling environment for GYW-led groups. A well connected and better resourced social movement for girls’ rights is able to promote a strong feminist counternarrative to the dominant patriarchal and ageist ideology. In the institutional domain, policy makers will develop greater awareness and knowledge about GYW inclusion in decision-making. Stronger connections between progressive policy makers and political leaders working at different levels will result in a coalition of reform-minded champions. In addition, pressure exercised by regional and international bodies will force national governments to take action and safeguard GYW’s rights to association and freedom of expression.

Within the population of girls and young women (between 14 till 24 years), the programme aims to strengthen the influence and participation of GYW who suffer most from (intersectional) discrimination and exclusion. These include: • GYW living in poor, remote rural areas and urban slums • GYW experiencing gender based violence (particularly girls who have married early) • GYW with disabilities • GYW who are out of school • Refugee and internally displaced GYW • GYW from sexual minority groups

title.narrative: Women's Rights and Gender Equality 521
# of CSOs (not youth or women led) with strengthened capacity to advance women’s rights and gender equality

comment.narrative: At the start of the programme, the value for this indicator is 0

Capacity support has been provided to Plan International Kenya to strenghten its capacity to effectively support GYW-groups and to provide direct financial support. Results are expected to materialize during 2023.

She Leads programme continued to build the capacity of CSOs within the gender sector working group to advocate for girls and young women rights. The programme has set the GYW agenda hence increasing their visibility, participation and inclusion in government-led process. This is a demonstraion of increased awareness of the rights for both GYW, CSOs and the duty bearers.

There has been an increase in the capacity of Plan International Kenya to deliver programs that are geared towards gender equality and GYW's rights. Frequent training sessions have resulted into a mind shift amongst senior management on building girls adn young women's agency. There is a greater realization for need to invest directly into GYW to support their advocacy work. This has resulted in a greater commitment by the management on resourcing informal girls' group to support their advocacy asks.

They have embraced the concept of working with GYW as partners and not as subjects of aid. Additionally, they are supporting legislation processes aimed at addressing GYW inclusion in decision making and leadership as well as on matters of development at the county level.

description.narrative: SL 2.2 Number of CSOs/CSO networks with increased GYW representation in active membership and/or leadership.

comment.narrative: At the start of the programme, the value for this indicator is 0

In the measurement of this indicator, we decided to focus only on the (contracted) first and second tier partners. In this case, of the CSO partner Pamoja CBO, we are witnessing a small-scale improvement: Pamoja CBO has committed to work with girls and young women as volunteers and employees in their programs to the extent of budget availability. The gains in organizational representativity achieved by the GYW-led groups and organizations which are supported by She Leads (but are not formally contracted) are reported in annex 3 of She Leads annual report.
Pamoja CBO (second tier partner) capacity strengthening has been reported in 2022

Pamoja CBO employed one GYW as the project associate in Jan 20232. The GYW doubles up as the County Lead GYW for Girls and Young Women in Kisumu. By empoying a GYW within their organization, Pamoja CBO has demonstrated that they are becoming a more gender sensitive organization. This has granted the GYW great milestone in regards to gaining legitimacy and credibility within the gender policy space in Kisumu. The GYW have utilized this platform to represent the interest of fellow Girl Advocates during the Gender sector forums and overall there is growing acceptance that the Gender Sector Working Group is a space for girls and young women as well.

This is the same CSO that was targeted since year two. Their current characteristics and representation enables the organization to play its role, hence no further changes would be required. However there's need for continued capacity strengthening

As a result of the She Leads support to County Technical Working Groups in Kisumu and Nairobi, CSOs working with GYW formed a coalition to create a strong network for lobby and advocacy on issues of GYW leadership and governance.

Plan and Pamoja CBO are the two organizations targetted to increase the representation of girls and young women in their constituent. Girls and young women will remain active members of these two organizations and will be involved in critical processes of project implementation, monitoring and evaluation.

title.narrative: # of CSOs which are both women & youth led that have enhanced representation of constituencies.

comment.narrative: At the start of the programme, the value for this indicator is 0
An update on the representational role and ability of the informal GYW-led groups supported by She Leads is presented in the She Leads narrative annual report 2023.

Plan Kenya and Pamoja CBO (the CSO partner) are giving intensive support and accompaniment to 34 GYW-led groups. However, these groups are not contracted as CSO partners. Therefore, they do not classify as second tier organizations. As a result, the value of this indicator is zero. The results (in terms of enhanced representation) achieved by the informal GYW-led groups are reported in annex 3 of the She Leads annual 2022 report.

The She leads programme increased the representation of GYW in the network by including one GYW group in the period under review. The group (Imarisha) is based in Mathare, Nairobi and comprises of 30 GYW aged between 18-24yrs. They are advocating for the rights of girls and young women on SRHR, GBV and economic empowernment issues. Plan Kenya worked with all the 23 groups as broken down. 16 GYW in Kisumu and 7 GYW in Nairobi. Of importance to note is that 22 GYW were already in the program so we only added one extra group in FY 2024.
Through the creation of space spaces and social media trainings, GYW-led groups managed to increase their outreach activities and to engage a larger group of GYW in their area

For 2025, additional 4 (3 in Kisumu, 1 in Mathare)GYW led groups will be brough on board to be part of She Leads project. She Leads anticipates that Many CSOs working with She Leads GYW either directly as implementing partners or indirectly will increase the representation of Girls and young women in their leadership structures. They will also ensure that GYW are active members of their processes, forums and are meaningfully engaged.

In setting the targets for this indicator, we included a larger group of CSOs which are influenced by She Leads advocacy. However, these CSOs are not formally contracted CSO partners and hence will not be counted as part of this indicator.
This indicator is about Plan International Kenya ability to fulfil its representational role towards the main stakeholders of the She Leads programme: girls and young women

Plan International Kenya has continued to evolve as an organization that champions the reights of GYW in all their diversities. To this extent, the organization is seen as an authority when it comes to leading agendas that relate to the empowerment of GYW. Similarly, the organization has demonstrated an inclusive approach that has seen girls and young women in all their diversities (refugees, urban, rural, survivors of SGBV, teenage mothers, disability) become key participants in all their programmes.
These CSO are part of the SGBV technical working groups in Kisumu and Nairobi Counties and have been trained on how to involve GYW in their lobby and advocacy
